feedback: For a correctly accepted point-down triangle: 'Right — turning it upside down didn't change the three straight sides, so it is still a triangle.'
For a correctly rejected curved-sided figure: 'Yes, and the reason matters: one side isn't straight, so it fails the test even though it looks pointy.'
If a learner rejects the long-thin triangle: 'Count the sides — three straight sides, closed. Being long and thin is a "doesn't-matter".'
If a learner calls the tilted square a 'diamond': 'Check the sides and corners — four equal straight sides and four square corners. Turning it didn't change those, so it is still a square.'
activities.intendedInsight: Membership of a shape category depends on invariant defining properties, and the reason given — not just the yes/no — shows whether a child is reasoning from properties or from the prototype.
learnerActions: Decide for each drawn figure whether it is or is not a given shape: non-prototypical positives (long-thin triangle, point-down triangle, tilted square) and near-miss negatives (one curved side, an open/unclosed corner).

For every decision, justify it by naming the defining property — e.g. 'three straight sides, all joined up' or 'that side isn't straight' — rather than 'it looks like one' or 'it points the right way'.
Compare a figure with one resized/recoloured and state whether anything that matters has changed.

Trace a finger along each side of a borderline figure to test 'how many sides?', 'is every side straight?' and 'is it joined up all the way round?' (and, for a square, 'are all four sides equal and all four corners square?')
activities.title: Is it or not? — and explain why

feedback: When the child cites a defining attribute: 'Good argument — four equal sides and square corners. The character gives in.'
If the child relies on how it points: 'The character will keep insisting — which way it points is a "doesn't-matter". Tell them about the sides and corners instead.'
When the child spots a missing feature: 'Exactly — you named what's broken, not just that it looks odd.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to defend a classification out loud with the defining attribute, against a plausible prototype-based objection, is the goal — the reasoning is what is being learned.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who holds up a rotated square and insists 'that's a diamond, not a square', arguing back from the four equal sides and square corners.
Answer repeated 'how do you know it's a triangle?' challenges, citing a defining attribute each time until the character concedes.
Handle thrown counterexamples — a curved-sided or unclosed figure — by explaining exactly which defining feature is missing.
Defend why size and colour changes do not change the shape's name.
activities.title: Shape detective: argue back

feedback: For a valid non-prototypical drawing: 'That looks very different from mine, but you kept three straight sides closed up — so it really is a triangle.'
For an open-cornered build: 'Right now it isn't closed. What would you do to join it up all the way round?'
If the child only draws the tidy prototype: 'Try one that is long and thin or points downward — can you still make it a real triangle?'
activities.intendedInsight: Producing a novel valid example — and justifying it — shows the child can apply the defining properties rather than only recognise a tidy prototype.
learnerActions: Draw a triangle that looks completely different from a given one but is still a triangle (e.g. long-thin, right, obtuse, or point-down), then explain why it still counts.
Build shapes from sticks or strips to a spec such as 'three straight sides, joined up all the way round'.
Make a near-miss on purpose (leave a corner open, or use a bendy side) and say what would have to change to fix it.
Turn your own cut-out shape, and compare it with a larger or smaller version, checking aloud that the defining attributes stay the same.
activities.title: Build and draw to a defining spec
